Four Forces. One Goal. Sustainable Growth.
TECHNOLOGY
The Unifying Force
PROFIT
Technology is the foundational enabler that connects and accelerates the other three Forces. Our digital-first operating model, with 90% of core applications on the cloud, powers the IRIS platform, which today serves 4.6 million+ customers. IRIS has evolved into a full-fledged retail super app with 250+ features, and adoption is deepening as 54% of mutual fund bookings and 71% of credit card EMI conversions now happen digitally. AI-powered chatbots deployed across customer journeys are improving service efficiency, accessibility, and personalisation, while advancing our commitment to paperless and green banking, and operational excellence.
Quality-led, Durable Profitability

Quality-led, Durable Profitability
At YES BANK, our profitability is being rebuilt on the pillars of resilience, diversification, and quality-led growth. The improvement in performance reflects a deliberate strategic shift towards a more granular, retail, and MSME-led portfolio, with a stronger focus on risk-adjusted returns, and increased risk discipline. Together, these shifts are aimed at building earnings that are more resilient across cycles – creating durable value for shareholders while supporting broader economic progress.
In FY 2025-26, YES BANK stepped decisively into its next phase of growth – marked by the onboarding of Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) as our largest shareholder and sharpening of operating model which is centred on tech-led franchise, quality-led underwriting, and granular deposit build-out. This is the foundation on which we are building a future-ready, differentiated bank anchored in sustainability, inclusion, and long-term value creation. Our Integrated Annual Report's theme "Four Forces. One Goal. Sustainable Growth." reflects this ambition and articulates the Bank's unified approach to delivering resilient economic, social and environmental outcomes.

At its core, our theme reinforces our commitment to the Triple Bottom Line - People, Planet and Profit - while positioning Technology as the fourth and unifying force that accelerates impact across all dimensions. Together, these forces converge towards one goal - sustainable growth that is inclusive, responsible, and future-ready.
PEOPLE
ONE GOAL
Empowering People, Expanding Access
PLANET
Our people agenda is built around three constituencies – our employees, our customers, and the communities that we serve. Through initiatives like YES Microfinance, the Bank has extended livelihood-linked credit to an active base of 6.92 lakh women borrowers in rural India, enabling pathways to financial independence and entrepreneurship. Internally, our Diversity, Equity, Inclusion & Belonging framework continues to shape a workplace where talent is nurtured and belonging is intentional. This has led to sustained recognition of being Great Place to Work®, for the fourth consecutive year. Our Score Kya Hua initiative has enabled lakhs of individuals to understand, build, improve and maintain their Credit Score, strengthening their long-term financial resilience.
Financing a Low-Carbon Future
Sustainable Growth

Sustainable Growth
Our environmental strategy is anchored in our commitment to Net Zero by 2030, supported by our disciplined, climate-aligned financing and responsible lending practices. Recognised as India’s highest-rated Bank in S&P Global CSA 2025, the Bank continues to strengthen its leadership in sustainable finance. With ` 7,690 crore of sanctioned facilities towards Renewable Energy projects in FY 2025-26, the Bank is actively enabling India’s transition towards a low-carbon economy.
These forces are not standalone priorities; they are interconnected drivers of the path ahead. Together, these forces enable the Bank to deliver on its unified goal of sustainable growth that balances purpose with performance, inclusion with innovation, and profitability with planetary responsibility. Through this framework, the Bank continues to demonstrate that purposeful banking is not only responsible banking, but also resilient and high-performing banking for the future.

It is with great pride and optimism that I present to you the Integrated Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26. Under his stewardship, the Bank navigated one of the most challenging periods in Indian banking and emerged fundamentally stronger - with strengthened governance, disciplined risk management, and a clear execution focus that will endure as a lasting legacy.

As your Bank enters its next chapter, we are confident that under his leadership, YES BANK is well-positioned to accelerate its growth trajectory, deepen client relationships, and build a truly resilient and future-ready institution. His vision of "One YES BANK", of integrating people, products, processes, and technology, aligns closely with the Board's strategic priorities for the Bank's next phase. FY 2025-26 MARKS THE BEGINNING OF A DEFINING NEW CHAPTER IN WHICH YOUR BANK WELCOMED A GLOBAL STRATEGIC PARTNER, COMPLETED A SEAMLESS LEADERSHIP TRANSITION, AND DELIVERED ITS HIGHEST ANNUAL PROFITABILITY SINCE RECONSTRUCTION.

Strategic Milestones SMBC Shareholding
FY 2025-26 marked a pivotal phase in your Bank’s evolution. The induction of Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) as your Bank’s largest shareholder, with a 24.9% stake, marked a landmark partnership. SMBC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMFG) - a globally systemically important bank and 2nd largest banking group of Japan, brings deep global expertise that will meaningfully augment your Bank’s capabilities in corporate banking, cross-border business, capital raising, and risk and governance frameworks. Macroeconomic Overview
As the only Indian Banking signatory to the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking, YES BANK is committed to support sustainable finance. The Bank in FY 2025-26 introduced Green Deposits to mobilise finance towards green activities, and continued to advance its target of achieving Net Zero operational emissions by 2030. For the fourth consecutive year, the Bank achieved the highest S&P Global ESG score among Indian banks and was the only Indian Bank to be included in the S&P Global Sustainability Yearbook 2026, with an ESG score of 79 out of 100. The Bank continued its inclusion in the FTSE4Good Index Series for the fourth consecutive year and won the ‘Most Sustainable Bank’ award as part of Business Today - India's Most Sustainable Companies Awards 2026.

India continued its trajectory as the fastest-growing major economy, with real GDP expanding by 7.7% in FY 2025-26. Growth was anchored by a strong revival in private consumption, which rose 7.7% during the year as compared with 5.8% in FY 2024-25, aided by the next-generation GST reforms that were rolled out in September 2025 to simplify rates and expand consumption headroom. Headline CPI inflation averaged 2.1% for the year, well below the RBI's medium-term target, supported by benign food inflation and stable core prices. Against this backdrop, the Reserve Bank of India undertook a calibrated easing cycle, reducing the policy repo rate cumulatively by 125 basis points since February 2025 to 5.25%, alongside liquidity infusion. This policy support translated into strong consumer demand, improving credit conditions, and a revival in private capital expenditure.
YOUR BANK CONTINUES TO BE AT THE FOREFRONT OF INDIA'S DIGITAL PAYMENTS REVOLUTION, PROCESSING NEARLY ONE IN EVERY THREE DIGITAL PAYMENT TRANSACTIONS IN THE COUNTRY, HANDLING APPROXIMATELY 19 BILLION TRANSACTIONS MONTHLY AND HOLDING LEADERSHIP POSITIONS ACROSS UPI, AEPS, NEFT, AND NACH.
Digital Banking and Innovation

Digital Banking and Innovation
Your Bank continues to be at the forefront of India's digital payments revolution, processing nearly one in every three digital payment transactions in the country, handling approximately 19 billion transactions monthly and holding leadership positions across UPI, AePS, NEFT, and NACH. The API-led banking ecosystem now comprises over 1,500 API-related products and services, while platforms such as IRIS, IRIS Biz, and YES Connect continue to drive client engagement and scalable growth. During the year, your Bank expanded its physical footprint with 82 new branches, alongside new digital initiatives such as Credit Line on UPI, IoT-based payments, biometric authentication, and the introduction of Green Fixed Deposits. The nationwide 'Score Kya Hua' financial literacy campaign delivered over 100 million cumulative reach, reinforcing your Bank’s role in advancing responsible credit behaviour at scale.
Corporate Social Responsibility

Corporate Social Responsibility
Despite this domestic resilience, the global environment remained challenging with ongoing conflict in West Asia, geopolitical fragmentation, and trade policy uncertainties weighing on growth. The IMF projects global growth to moderate to 3.1% in 2026. Looking ahead, India remains the fastest-growing major economy, with the RBI projecting GDP growth at 6.6% for FY 2026-27, providing a supportive backdrop for your Bank's continued expansion.
Through YES Foundation, your Bank continued to advance its 3Es strategy - Employability, Entrepreneurship, and Environmental Sustainability. Cumulatively, your Bank's CSR programmes have trained over 8,000 youth, empowered over 21,000 rural entrepreneurs and driven substantial environmental restoration by planting over 2 lakh trees, reinforcing its commitment to inclusive and sustainable growth.

Financial Performance
Looking Ahead

Looking Ahead
Your Bank reported a Net Profit of ` 3,476 crore, its highest annual profitability since reconstruction, reflecting a 44.5% growth over FY 2024-25 - a direct outcome of disciplined execution and strategic clarity. Your Bank exited Q4 FY 2025-26 at an annualised Return on Assets (RoA) of 1.0%, with a full year RoA expanding to 0.8% from 0.6% in FY 2024-25. Total deposits crossed the landmark ` 3 lakh crore mark, with Retail and Branch Banking deposits contributing 58.4% and growing at 13.5% Y-O-Y, outpacing both the industry (10.2%) and private sector banks (11.4%). CASA balances crossed the milestone of ` 1 lakh crore. Your Bank's Advances book rose to ` 273,445 crore, registering 11.1% Y-O-Y growth, underpinned by strong disbursement momentum across segments. Borrowings declined 9.4% Y-O-Y to ` 64,864 crore, aided by a sustained reduction in RIDF-related balances, as your Bank achieved another year of NIL shortfalls across all key Priority Sector Lending (PSL) sub-categories.

As we look to the future, your Bank is well positioned for sustained value creation. With a strengthened balance sheet, a strategic global partnership with SMBC, an industry-leading digital platform, and a stable experienced leadership team, your Bank remains committed to delivering sustainable and profitable growth. While external risks from the global environment persist, India's structural strengths and the Bank's disciplined approach provide confidence in our ability to navigate uncertainty and capitalise on emerging opportunities.

Operating Environment

Operating Environment
The global economy in FY 2025-26 was characterised by a balance between resilience and volatility, as geopolitical conflicts and policy uncertainty influenced international markets. The IMF anticipates a moderation in global growth to 3.1% in 2026, with downside risks from geopolitical fragmentation and resurfacing trade tensions.

Strengthening the Digital Lending Ecosystem
Consolidated and Harmonised Regulatory Framework
The RBI introduced a series of measures aimed at strengthening risk management and improving credit discipline while enabling more efficient credit flow. These included the Prudential Framework for Project Finance, which established distinct treatment for construction and operational phases with corresponding provisioning requirements; the Framework for Co-lending Arrangements, which broadened the scope of co-lending with a minimum risk-retention requirement and enhanced disclosure standards; and revised directions on non-fund-based credit facilities - covering guarantees, electronic guarantees, co-acceptance of bills and Partial Credit Enhancement - that both consolidated existing norms and widened funding avenues for infrastructure

The RBI issued the Digital Lending Directions, 2025, consolidating earlier guidelines and strengthening governance, transparency and customer protection across digital lending models. The Directions introduced enhanced requirements for Lending Service Provider arrangements, borrower disclosures, cooling-off periods, customer consent mechanisms and mandatory reporting of all Digital Lending Apps on the RBI’s CIMS portal, reinforcing regulatory focus on responsible innovation and customer-centric digital lending practices
India’s digital payments ecosystem continued to expand rapidly during FY 2025-26, driven by increasing smartphone penetration, growing merchant acceptance infrastructure and widespread adoption of real-time payment systems. UPI transaction volumes continued to grow strongly, while digital payments increasingly became the preferred mode of transaction across retail and business segments. The continued formalisation of the economy and increasing adoption of digital commerce further strengthened the role of digital payments within the financial ecosystem

In FY 2025-26, the Reserve Bank of India undertook one of its most significant regulatory exercises in recent years, issuing consolidated Master Directions in November 2025, bringing together multiple standalone regulations across credit facilities, credit risk and concentration risk management, income recognition and asset classification, capital adequacy, governance, investment portfolio classification, asset-liability management, financial statements and disclosures, CRR/ SLR requirements, resource raising, securitisation and outsourcing risk management. The move aims to enhance regulatory consistency, improve clarity of interpretation and simplify compliance across the banking sector
AI, Data and Cyber Resilience
Digital Public Infrastructure and Financial Innovation
Artificial Intelligence, advanced analytics and automation continued to transform banking operations, customer engagement and risk management practices globally. As digital transactions scaled, cybersecurity, fraud management, data governance and operational resilience grew correspondingly important. During the year, a series of RBI measures reinforced digital trust, strengthened Payment Aggregator requirements, enhanced due diligence for Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AePS) operators, mandatory two-factor authentication, and migration to the exclusive 'bank.in' domain to curb phishing and spoofing

India’s Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) continued to evolve as a global benchmark for technology-led financial inclusion and innovation. Initiatives such as the Account Aggregator framework, Unified Lending Interface (ULI), Aadhaar-enabled services and Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) continued to expand opportunities for digital onboarding, consent-based data-sharing, credit assessment and customer servicing. Mission Digital ShramSetu, a proposed national AI-driven ecosystem to enhance financial security, market access, and formal skilling, was put forward by NITI Aayog in October 2025
Liquidity, Capital and Market Risk Management
Customer Protection and Related Party Oversight
During the year, RBI guidelines focussed on enhancing transparency in financial transactions, strengthening fraud risk management, ensuring fair interest-charging practices, expanding the treatment of wilful and large defaulters, managing inoperative accounts & unclaimed deposits, preventing financial frauds via voice calls and SMS, and strengthening nomination coverage. Governance standards were further reinforced through the revised Related Party Lending Framework, introducing expanded definitions, Board-level oversight, materiality thresholds and safeguards against indirect or reciprocal lending arrangements

The regulatory focus on balance sheet resilience continued through amendments to the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) framework, including additional run-off assumptions for internet and mobile banking-enabled deposits and revised treatment of Government Securities used as High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA), effective April 2026. Separately, the RBI introduced an enabling framework for capital market exposures - permitting acquisition finance by banks, easing limits on lending against shares and other instruments, and adopting a principle-based approach for lending to capital market intermediaries - balancing wider credit opportunities with appropriate prudential safeguards

Increasing Demand for Personalisation and Convenience
Customers increasingly prefer digital channels for onboarding, servicing, payments and day-to-day banking interactions. Widespread smartphone adoption, internet penetration and increasing familiarity with digital financial services have accelerated the shift towards self-service, always-on banking experiences. At the same time, customers continue to expect seamless integration across physical and digital channels, driving the need for omnichannel engagement models

India continued to advance its energy transition agenda through investments in renewable energy, transmission infrastructure, energy storage, clean mobility and emerging low-carbon technologies. Having achieved key milestones under its earlier Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) ahead of schedule, including sourcing nearly 50% of installed power capacity from non-fossil fuel sources, India strengthened its climate ambitions through its updated 2031-35 NDCs, with enhanced targets relating to emissions intensity reduction, non-fossil fuel capacity and carbon sequestration
Climate risk management continued to gain prominence within the financial sector as regulators increasingly focussed on strengthening resilience to physical and transition risks. During the year, the RBI advanced its climate risk agenda through pilot exercises on climate risk, including SMA/NPA considerations, while also undertaking capacity-building initiatives to enhance climate risk management capabilities across regulated entities. The launch of the RBI Climate Risk Information System (RBI-CRIS) in May 2025 further strengthened climate-related data availability and risk assessment, supporting more informed financing and risk-management decisions

Customer expectations continue to evolve beyond traditional banking services towards personalised, intuitive and context-driven experiences. Advances in data analytics, Artificial Intelligence and digital ecosystems are enabling more tailored product offerings, faster decision-making and proactive customer engagement. Increasing competition from digital-first financial service providers has further elevated expectations around speed, convenience and service quality
Expanding Financial Inclusion and Accessibility
Strengthening Customer Protection and Transparency
Financial inclusion continues to remain a key national priority, supported by digital public infrastructure, increasing formalisation and expanding access to financial services. During the year, the RBI strengthened accessibility requirements under Video KYC guidelines, including measures to improve onboarding experiences for persons with disabilities. Continued adoption of digital channels and simplified customer journeys is helping extend financial services to a broader customer base

RBI’s Master Direction on Responsible Business Conduct consolidated guidelines on customer service, inoperative accounts, lockers, and Basic Savings Bank Deposit Accounts. Regulatory focus on customer protection and transparency continued to strengthen through expanded nomination facilities, simplified deceased claim settlement processes, removal of pre-payment charges on floating-rate loans for individuals and Micro and Small Enterprises, revised KYC requirements and strengthening of the Internal Ombudsman Framework
Sustainability reporting expectations continued to mature during the year, with increasing emphasis on consistency, comparability and decision-useful disclosures for investors and stakeholders. Regulatory developments, including the phased expansion of sustainability disclosure and assurance requirements by SEBI, continued to strengthen ESG reporting practices among listed entities. These developments are driving greater transparency around sustainability performance, governance practices and long-term value creation, while enabling more informed capital allocation decisions across the financial ecosystem

Sustainable and transition finance continued to gain momentum across the financial sector, supported by increasing investments in renewable energy, clean mobility, green buildings and climate-resilient infrastructure. During the year, the sustainable finance ecosystem evolved through enhanced greenhouse gas emission intensity disclosures under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) for designated entities and the introduction of the IFSCA’s Transition Bond Framework to support credible decarbonisation pathways. In parallel, green bond issuances by domestic financial institutions reflected growing investor appetite for climate-aligned assets and diversified sources of sustainable capital

Building Resilience through Continuous Assessment

Building Resilience through Continuous Assessment
Risk appetite acts as an articulation and allocation of the quantum of risk that the Bank is willing to assume through its business activities, in pursuit of its strategic objectives and desired returns. Risk Appetite is duly set and monitored by the Enterprise Risk Management Committee (ERMC), Risk Management Committee (RMC) and the Board, and is integrated into Bank’s Strategy, Business, Risk and Capital plans. Risk appetite is the Bank’s benchmark for balancing return and risk, recognising a range of outcomes in the course of business. It is expressed in both quantitative and qualitative parameters, and considers economic conditions, events and outcomes to reflect potential impact on earnings, capital, funding or liquidity. Risk Appetite is set at Bank-wide level, and is further translated to operational limit for portfolios, business, and risk units, by means of respective Board-approved policies viz. Enterprise Risk Management Policy, ALM Policy, Market Risk Policy, Credit Risk Policy and Operational Risk Management Policy, among others.

The Bank conducts a detailed Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) review exercise, which is approved by the Board at least on an annual basis to identify and undertake assessment of the Bank’s risk universe. The Board has the overall responsibility for Risk Management and oversees the Bank’s risk universe, reviews its risk appetite in line with business strategy, and assess its internal controls and mitigation measures in place for the risks and capital requirements. The Bank performs sensitivity analysis/ stress testing through its Board-approved Stress Testing framework based on regulatory guidelines and industry best practices. The results of these tests are presented to the ERMC and RMC/Board on a quarterly basis. As per the risk-based audit plan, approved by the Audit Committee of the Board, various functions get audited at a frequency laid out in the plan. The audit of risk function has been done in FY 2024-25 as well as in FY 2025-26.

YES BANK’s ability to create sustainable value is influenced not only by its strategy and execution, but also by its ability to understand and respond to the expectations of stakeholders. As a financial institution operating at the intersection of economic development, financial inclusion, digital transformation and sustainable finance, YES BANK engages with a diverse set of stakeholders whose decisions, expectations and actions influence the Bank’s operating environment, risk profile and long-term success.
Based on an assessment undertaken by the Bank’s senior management and leadership teams, ten stakeholder groups have been identified as having the most significant influence on, and being most significantly impacted by, the Bank’s operations, products, services and value creation activities.

Stakeholders play a critical role in shaping the context within which the Bank operates. Customers influence product innovation and service delivery. Regulators shape the governance and compliance landscape. Investors determine access to capital. Financial and ESG analysts shape market perception and credibility. The media influences public discourse and reputation. Employees drive organisational capability and culture. Communities, industry bodies, suppliers and business partners contribute to the broader ecosystem within which the Bank creates value.

Insights generated through stakeholder engagement serve as important inputs into the Bank’s strategic planning process, risk management framework, sustainability agenda and materiality assessment. The Bank follows a robust stakeholder engagement model, employing a combination of structured and need-based engagement mechanisms to reach out to these stakeholder groups on a periodic basis. The Bank has set up dedicated grievance redressal mechanisms and specialised business units, through which stakeholders can raise their grievances. Critical concerns voiced by stakeholders are communicated to relevant Board-level committees, periodically.
As stakeholder expectations continue to evolve, maintaining a continuous dialogue with these groups becomes essential for identifying emerging opportunities, anticipating risks and ensuring that strategic priorities remain aligned with changing needs and expectations. Stakeholder engagement therefore serves as an important mechanism through which the Bank gathers insights, validates priorities and strengthens its understanding of the issues that are most relevant to its long-term success.

Materiality Assessment
YES BANK’s value creation is shaped by a broad set of economic, regulatory, social, technological and sustainability-related developments. Shifting customer expectations, macroeconomic conditions and societal priorities collectively influence the opportunities and challenges facing the Bank. While numerous factors have the potential to affect business performance and stakeholder perceptions, not all issues influence value creation equally. To ensure that management attention, resources and strategic actions remain focussed on the areas that matter most, YES BANK undertakes a structured materiality assessment process on a periodic basis.

reviewed annually, including in FY 2025-26. Following the review, the Sustainability Council and the Corporate Social Responsibility & Environmental Social and Governance (CSR & ESG) Committee of the Board reaffirmed that the identified material topics continue to appropriately reflect the Bank’s operating context, stakeholder priorities and value creation objectives. Accordingly, no changes were made to the material topics during FY 2025-26.
Materiality assessment serves as an important link between stakeholder expectations, strategic decision-making, risk management and value creation. It helps the Bank understand which issues require the greatest focus, where resources should be allocated and how emerging opportunities and risks should be addressed. The assessment also provides a framework for aligning business priorities with stakeholder expectations while strengthening the Bank’s ability to respond to a changing operating environment.
Preparing for an Enhanced Assessment
Our Double Materiality Approach1

Our Double Materiality Approach1
In light of evolving global and domestic regulations, including International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) S1: General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information, SEBI’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting framework, and RBI’s Draft Disclosure framework on Climate-related Financial Risks, which call for a more integrated approach for identifying material issues that links sustainability issues with their current and potential financial implications, the Bank aims to conduct a fresh and enhanced Materiality Assessment in FY 2026-27 that incorporates both impact and financial materiality dimensions into the assessment approach.

Recognising the increasing interdependence between sustainability performance and business performance, the Bank applies a Double Materiality approach. This approach enables the Bank to evaluate material issues from two complementary perspectives. The first perspective considers the impact of the Bank’s activities, products, services and business relationships on the economy, environment and society, including impacts on human rights. The second perspective evaluates how sustainability-related issues may influence the Bank’s strategy, operations, risk profile, financial performance and long-term enterprise value. By considering both dimensions, the Bank gains a more comprehensive understanding of the issues that are most relevant to stakeholders and most critical to long-term business success.
Materiality Matrix

Materiality Matrix
The materiality matrix represents the outcome of the Bank’s materiality assessment process. The matrix maps identified topics based on a plotting of Importance to External Stakeholders on the Y-axis and the Importance to Enterprise Value Creation on the X-axis. The median rating has been taken to be the materiality threshold for both aspects. 11 out of 15 topics rated on or above the median were determined as the Bank’s most significant material topics. Therefore, topics positioned in the upper-right quadrant represent the issues that are most significant to both stakeholders and the Bank’s long-term value creation process.
The material topics identified through this assessment process represent the issues that have the highest significance for stakeholders and the strongest influence on the Bank’s ability to create sustainable value. These topics provide important inputs into strategic planning, risk management, stakeholder engagement, sustainability initiatives, capital allocation decisions and performance management processes. Environmental Stewardship
Ensuring Operational Eco-efficiency
With an extensive network of branches and offices serving diverse sections of society across India, YES BANK recognises the importance of managing its ecological footprint responsibly and continues to take focussed measures to minimise the environmental impact of its operations. Through a structured, independently certified ISO 14001:2015 Environmental Management System (EMS) covering 1,289 facilities, the Bank embeds disciplined environmental practices across its operations. This enables it to conserve resources, improve efficiency, reduce waste and greenhouse-gas emissions, and advance steadily towards its target of achieving net-zero operational emissions by 2030.

In FY 2025-26, the Bank bolstered its environmental performance across key dimensions of its operations. It successfully completed its 13th year of EMS certification maintaining the distinction of possessing the highest number of ISO 14001:2015 certified facilities amongst the Banking & Financial Services and the Insurance (BFSI) sector, globally. As a result of its concerted efforts across improvements in data collection and tracking, reduced dependence on DG set usage, and upgradation to energy-efficient equipment, the Bank in FY 2025-26, reduced its total energy consumption by 4.19%, achieved 14.48% lower Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions compared to the previous year, and reduced its emission intensity per Full Time Employee (FTE) by 17.04%, to 0.98 tCO2e. As of March 31, 2026, 83 of the Bank’s facilities have been transitioned to renewable energy, with renewables representing 21.57% of its electricity mix in FY 2025-26, resulting in avoided emissions of around 7,493 tCO₂e.

The Bank’s approach to operational eco-efficiency is anchored in its Environmental Management Policy, overseen by the CSR & ESG Committee of the Board and the executive-level Sustainability Council, and delivered through a robust ISO 14001:2015-certified Environmental Management System. The Bank works to conserve natural resources, transition its facilities to renewable energy (RE), manage waste responsibly, and drive down the emissions and energy intensity of its own operations. Its environmental agenda is organised around four mutually reinforcing pillars described below.

Integrating Environmental & Social Risk into Lending
Responsible lending is central to YES BANK’s approach to sustainability. Since 2006, the Bank has voluntarily implemented an Environment & Social Policy (ESP), based on international frameworks such as IFC Performance Standards, that embeds environmental and social risk assessment directly into its credit decisions, ensuring the projects it finances are evaluated for their impact on people and the planet, not only their financial returns.

In FY 2025-26, the Bank strengthened its ESMS by applying risk-based due diligence across its lending portfolio, completing E&S reviews for 148 transactions. High-risk exposures underwent enhanced expert review, climate-risk screening and negative screening against IFC Exclusion List-based prohibited activities, reinforcing responsible financing boundaries.
YES BANK’s Environmental and Social Policy helps ensure that the Bank’s lending decisions consider environmental and social (E&S) risks, not just financial and credit risks. Responsible lending is part of the Bank’s risk management approach and supports reputation management, stakeholder confidence and sustainable business growth. To integrate E&S considerations into its lending processes, the Bank screens activities against the Bank’s policy requirements, applies a risk-based due diligence framework that evaluates project transactions for potential environmental and social impacts and incorporates appropriate mitigation measures where necessary. By embedding E&S considerations into credit appraisal and decision-making, YES BANK seeks to promote responsible business practices, manage potential risks proactively and support the transition towards a more sustainable and resilient economy.

Promoting Green Finance
YES BANK has long been a pioneer of green finance in India, issuing the country’s maiden Green Bond in 2015. As India progresses towards its net-zero goals, the Bank channelises capital towards renewable energy, clean transport and green buildings, amongst other climate-aligned sectors, helping its clients adapt and thrive in a low-carbon, resource-efficient economy.
In FY 2025-26, the Bank sanctioned ` 7,690 crore of debt financing for renewable energy projects, spanning solar, wind, hybrid and pumped-storage capacity of approximately 1,812 MW. This takes the Bank’s cumulative renewable energy financing since 2015 to ` 52,951 crore across roughly 11.92 GW. The Bank also launched its Green Deposit product and continued to expand its financing towards electric vehicle and rooftop solar lending, and continued to operate as one of only five accredited entities for the Green Climate Fund in India.

The Bank’s green-finance strategy combines innovative financial mechanisms with targeted lending to climate-aligned sectors and active market-building. Through Green Deposits and its accreditation to the Green Climate Fund, the Bank mobilises capital towards sustainable outcomes; through dedicated products it finances renewable energy, electric mobility and rooftop solar; and drives case-led innovations to de-risk and scale emerging clean-energy models for the wider market. The Group provides for gratuity, for all employees. Gratuity is payable to an employee in accordance with the Payment of Gratuity Act. The Group accounts for the liability for future gratuity benefits using the projected unit cost method based on independent actuarial valuation. The defined gratuity benefit plans are valued by an independent actuary as on the Balance Sheet date using the projected unit credit method as per the requirement of Accounting Standard-15, Employee Benefits, to determine the present value of the defined benefit obligation and the related service costs. Under this method, the determination is based on actuarial calculations, which include assumptions about demographics, early retirement, salary increases and interest rates. Actuarial gain or loss is recognised in the Profit and Loss account. The current employee Gratuity liability as at March 31, 2026 is ` 331.01 crore. Assets set aside by the Bank to meet this liability as on March 31, 2026 stands at ` 111.76 crore*

The Bank is registered with the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner (RPFC) for managing benefits under the Employee Provident Fund and the Employee Pension Scheme. All employees of the Group are covered under the Employees Provident Fund, a defined contribution plan in which both the employee and the Bank contribute on a monthly basis. The employee contributes 12% of monthly basic wages towards the Provident Fund and employer contributes 3.67% of the monthly basic wages to the Provident Fund. Employee Pension Scheme is a mandatory retirement plan wherein the Group as employer contributes on behalf of employees on a monthly basis with the maximum contribution limited to ` 1,250. Employees with basic wages up to ` 15,000 per month are mandatorily covered under the scheme. Employees who currently draw basic wages of more than ` 15,000 per month, however, were part of Pension scheme earlier

Advancing Financial Inclusion and Social Finance
For YES BANK, financial inclusion is both a strategic priority and an important way to contribute to India’s development. Through an extensive last-mile network and a microfinance programme that has cumulatively disbursed over ` 19,550 crore to over 43 lakh families since inception, the Bank aims to bring unbanked, hard-to-reach and vulnerable communities into the formal financial system, in an effort to reduce inequality and advance India's sustainable development goals.

In FY 2025-26, the Bank deepened financial inclusion across channels. It served over 3.24 lakh customers through 668 Business Correspondent Branches, and a further 3.3 lakh rural customers through 249 Business Correspondent Banking Outlets (BCBOs). Through YES Microfinance, it disbursed ` 1,841.73 crore to over 3 lakh women, supporting an active base of 6.92 lakh women borrowers, and extended ` 4,638 crore to microfinance institutions for on-lending. The Bank opened 1.13 lakh new PMJDY accounts, empowered over 15,000 women through financial literacy drives across 1,300 branches, and extended its digital reach with a 28.27% share of Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AePS) transactions.
The Bank’s approach to advancing financial inclusion is driven and overseen by its highest governance body, with the Board of Directors regularly reviewing the progress on financial inclusion initiatives through quarterly updates. Working through dedicated divisions such as Inclusive and Social Banking (ISB) and Microfinance Banking (MFB) and an extensive last-mile Business Correspondent network, the Bank adopts a holistic, multi-pronged approach, offering a comprehensive bouquet of financial solutions tailored to the unique needs of bottom-of-the-pyramid (BOP) customers. Its initiatives are organised around four priority areas, detailed below.

Social Finance 4
YES KHUSHI Home Loans primarily cater to customers from the Economically Weaker Section and Low Income Group segments who may have formal, semi-formal or informal income documentation and require financial assistance to buy or construct their homes. The Bank’s target customers include small traders and shopkeepers, blue-collar employees, and employees of MSMEs and private firms, many of whom may not have formal income documents or may receive their income or salary in cash.
Understanding these challenges, YES BANK launched YES KHUSHI Home Loans in May 2016 as part of its commitment to social responsibility and financial inclusion. The programme is designed to help individuals from economically weaker and low-income households fulfil their aspiration of owning or constructing a home.

The Bank recognises that finance is a powerful lever for inclusive development, and that channelling capital towards priority sectors is essential for creating long-term value. Through its focus on social finance, the Bank directs funding to sectors that contribute significantly to India’s Sustainable Development Goals. It supports agriculture value chain that sustains rural India, finances small and medium enterprises that power the economy and create jobs, and extends affordable housing loans to the economically weaker and low-income households for whom home ownership has long remained out of reach.
Taken together, these four priority areas describe a single, coherent commitment: to widen access at the last mile, to lend inclusively and responsibly, to build financial literacy that makes inclusion durable, and to channel social finance towards the sectors that power equitable growth. In doing so, the Bank aims to advance both India’s development goals and its own long-term, sustainable value creation.
As at March 31, 2026, the Bank’s YES KHUSHI (affordable) home-loan portfolio stood at ~` 8,133 crore, with nearly 55,343 customers extended loans under the programme.

Impact Story

Impact Story
Chimdiben, from Jalkheda block in Barwani, Madhya Pradesh, owned 2.5 acres of land in an area largely dependent on rain-fed agriculture. Erratic rainfall and the absence of irrigation restricted farmers to a single Kharif crop, resulting in low yields, unstable incomes and widespread seasonal migration. Due to acute water scarcity, Chimdiben could cultivate only part of her land during the monsoon, making farming insufficient to sustain her family.
Her challenges included complete dependence on rainfall, single-crop farming with low productivity, annual farm income of only ` 35,000, no scope for Rabi or summer cultivation, seasonal migration for wage labour, frequent disruption in her children’s education, and limited access to technical knowledge and improved agricultural practices.
Through the project, Chimdiben gained access to interventions focussed on water security, skills and crop diversification, including capacity building and training, well rejuvenation, a solar lift irrigation system, and crop diversification and intensification. Her transition from rain-fed subsistence farming to diversified, year-round agriculture demonstrates how integrated water, energy and livelihood interventions can enhance farm income and enable income-led rural transformation. The Bank operates a comprehensive Enterprise Risk Governance framework with the overall responsibility for risk resting with the Board and Board-level committees, including the Risk Management Committee ('RMC'), Audit Committee of the Board ('ACB'), Special Committee of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of Frauds (‘SCBMF’), Review Committee for Classification and Declaration of Wilful Defaulters ('Review Committee') and Board Credit Committee ('BCC'). YES BANK recognises that responsible procurement is central to building a resilient, ethical and sustainable banking ecosystem. The Bank’s environmental and social footprint extends well beyond its own operations into a diverse value chain. Its Value‑Chain Engagement Programme, guided by SEBI’s BRSR and BRSR Core frameworks, covered top upstream partners representing 29.77% of total purchases by value. The programme combined ESG surveys, capacity‑building sessions on the Bank’s ESG Supplier Code and BRSR requirements, and data validation to improve supplier preparedness and disclosure quality.

Principles for Responsible Banking: Portfolio Impact Assessment and Targets

In 2019, YES BANK, together with 32 global banks and UNEP FI, co-founded the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB), the world’s first global framework designed to align banking practices with the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Climate Agreement. Today, the PRB has expanded to over 360 global signatories, collectively representing approximately 50% of global banking assets. YES BANK continues to remain the only Indian Founding Signatory, reinforcing its commitment towards sustainable and climate-aligned development. Under the PRB framework, banks are required to conduct comprehensive portfolio impact analyses to understand how their financing activities interact and to minimise negative impacts and maximise positive impacts of their businesses.

The Monetary Policy Committee responded to the changing inflation-growth dynamics with a calibrated easing cycle during FY 2025-26. The cycle began in February 2025 with a 25 bps reduction in the repo rate and a shift in stance from accommodative to neutral. In June, the MPC front-loaded easing through a 50 bps repo rate cut and a phased 100 bps reduction in the Cash Reserve Ratio. Following cumulative repo rate reductions of 100 bps, the stance returned to neutral to preserve policy flexibility. A further 25 bps repo rate cut in December brought the repo rate to 5.25%, where it remained until the April 2026 meeting.

External Sector and Currency Movement
India enters FY 2026-27 with a resilient domestic growth base, even as the external environment remains uncertain. Growth is expected to be supported by domestic demand, services-sector momentum, healthy corporate and banking balance sheets, policy support and ample system liquidity. At the same time, global trade fragmentation, commodity-price volatility, capital-flow uncertainty and potential weather-related disruptions remain key risks.

Risk Management
Internal Audit
The Bank’s long-term financial security and success is built on its risk management architecture. The Bank’s risk management is based on three lines of defence: (a) business units, (b) independent control functions, and (c) internal audit.
The Bank also subjects its operations to concurrent auditing by reputed audit firms to complement its internal auditing function. Concurrent auditing covers core activities, operations (including credit), financial markets, data centres (including IT & IS systems) and branches in compliance with regulatory guidelines. All audit reports are circulated to the relevant management teams and the ACB.

The Bank’s Internal Audit Department (IAD), which is ISO 9001:2015 certified (Quality Management System), provides an independent and objective assurance and consulting services to add value and improve its risk and control environment. The IAD monitors the adequacy, effectiveness and adherence to internal controls, processes and procedures instituted by the Bank’s management and extant regulations.
Further, the Bank’s Board has the overall responsibility of risk management, with the risk management architecture being overseen by the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board. Additionally, risk management is undertaken by other Board-level committees for respective risks as per the Bank’s Board-approved risk architecture.
Sustainable Finance

Sustainable Finance
The Sustainable Finance (SF) function is responsible for integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) considerations into the Bank’s business activities. The team works to align the Bank’s practices with national and global sustainability frameworks, including the National Guidelines for Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC), the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Paris Climate Agreement and the Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB). In coordination with Sustainability SPOCs across various functions, SF supports the implementation of the Bank’s sustainability strategy and the achievement of ESG related goals as guided by the Sustainability Council, chaired by the MD & CEO. The function also steers and provides periodic updates on the Bank’s ESG performance to the Board-level CSR & ESG Committee.

To further this objective, the Chief Compliance Officer at the Bank reports directly to the ACB.

The Bank has put in place a system viz. Action Point Tracker System to track actionable emanating from Board/Board Level Committee meetings. Action Taken Report on the decisions taken/directions in a meeting is placed at the succeeding meeting(s) of the Board/Board Level Committees.

Each Committee is guided by its Terms of Reference, which provides for the scope, powers and duties and responsibilities. (i) Policy on Appointment of Directors:
During the year under review, Company Secretary, acted as the Secretary to the Board level Committees. The eleven (11) Board Level Committees are briefly described below:
The Bank has deployed a structured and robust framework for identifying, building, and developing talent pipeline of successors in critical roles. The successors are identified using assessment centre methodology comprising of scientifically valid tools like psychometric assessment, behavioural event interview, role play, case study analysis and 360-degree feedback. Developmental inputs are provided to build leadership capabilities and strengthen internal talent pipeline. The succession list is reviewed periodically to keep it current and contextual for any exclusions/inclusions as deemed necessary.

The Directors are presented with important/critical information on the operations of the Bank as well as information which requires deliberations at the highest level. The Board has complete access to all the relevant information within the Bank and also has access to the top management of the Bank and any additional information to make informed and timely decisions. All board and committee meetings are governed by structured agenda notes which are backed by comprehensive background papers along with relevant annexures. As a part of green initiative by the Bank, all relevant agenda papers pertaining to the Board/ Committee meetings are being circulated well in advance to the Board of Directors through web-based portal to facilitate easy access of agenda on iPad which would provide sufficient time to the Board for reading and understanding the proposals placed at the meeting.

The Bank has a Board approved ‘Policy on Board Diversity and Fit & Proper Criteria and Succession Planning’ (‘Fit & Proper Policy’) which comprises of diversity of Board’s composition, succession planning and the detailed process for appointment of Directors including the required skill sets, experience, qualification, etc. as required under the Act, SEBI LODR, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and other regulatory and business requirements. The Nomination & Remuneration Committee is being guided by the said policy, while recommending appointment of Directors. As per the Fit & Proper Policy of the Bank, Bank ensures that not less than 51% of the total number of members of the Board of Directors shall have special knowledge or practical experience in (i) accountancy, (ii) agriculture and rural economy, (iii) banking, (iv) co-operation, (v) economics, (vi) finance, (vii) law, (viii) small-scale industry, (ix) Information Technology (x) Payment & Settlement Systems (xi) Human Resources (xii) Risk Management (xiii) Business Management (xiv) any other matter the special knowledge of, and practical experience in, which would, in the opinion of RBI, be useful to the Bank.

8. Mechanisms to prevent adverse consequences to the complainant in discrimination and harassment cases.
The Bank has implemented a web-based ‘Corporate Whistle Blower Initiative’ (CWI) portal which is an independent online reporting service aimed at facilitating secure and confidential communication between complainants and the organization. The Bank has also set up Internal Committees to investigate sexual harassment complaints in line with the Bank’s policy on Prevention of Sexual Harassment at Workplace (POSH). All complaints are investigated in an impartial and confidential manner, with any form of retaliation against complainants strictly prohibited and subject to disciplinary action. The salient features of the POSH policy and the details of the Internal Committees are shared with all employees and displayed at branches and offices of the Bank.

5. Describe the internal mechanisms in place to redress grievances related to human rights issues.
Grievances related to human rights can be raised through the Bank’s ‘Corporate Whistle Blower Initiative’ (CWI) portal (using the organization code “YESCARE”), which is an independent online reporting service aimed at facilitating secure and confidential communication between the Whistle Blower and the independent Whistleblower Committee constituted by the Bank. Any grievances related to violations of human rights can also be reported to the Bank appointed Liaison Officer, details of which are provided in the Bank’s Human Rights Policy available on the Bank’s website. All grievances received are evaluated and routed to relevant Committees for guidance, suitable action and appropriate closure.
As per the Bank’s Code of Conduct, every employee is required to uphold and maintain the dignity of other executives working in the Bank. They should maintain a productive work environment that is free from sexual harassment. Those who violate this Code of Conduct may be subject to disciplinary action, including possible dismissal.

2. Details of the scope and coverage of any Human rights due diligence conducted.

2. Details of the scope and coverage of any Human rights due diligence conducted.
The Bank conducted an independent human rights due diligence exercise aimed at assessing the Bank’s policies and processes, identifying potential human rights related risks, implementing measures to prevent human rights violations, maintaining compliance with legal standards, and promoting ethical practices within the Bank’s operations. The human rights assessments and the associated due diligence covered eight critical aspects of human rights, essential for maintaining ethical and fair workplace practices, viz. child labour, discrimination, freedom of association and collective bargaining, fair remuneration, fair working hours, occupational health and safety, bonded labour, workers’ involvement and protection of human rights. The process involved interactions and interviews with a diverse group of stakeholders, including senior management, employees from various departments, contractors, housekeeping staff, and security staff, ensuring comprehensive information gathering across different levels of the organization. The assessment covered the Bank’s corporate office, YES BANK House and a branch in Mumbai. In FY 2025-26, the Bank expanded the coverage of its human rights assessment to 140 additional Branches.

Some large projects financed by the Bank generate carbon emissions, which if unmitigated or unchecked may contribute to increasing global warming. In FY 2021-22, YES BANK emerged as the first Indian Bank to measure and report financed emissions of its fund-based electricity generation portfolio. In FY 2022-23, the Sustainability Council approved decarbonisation targets to reduce the financed emissions intensity of the Bank’s fund-based electricity generation portfolio, in line with the well below 2 degrees, striving for 1.5-degree scenario. Since then, the Bank has expanded the scope of its financed emission measurement and disclosure to include the cement (manufacturing) and iron & steel (manufacturing) portfolio (covering corporate loans, investment (treasury), and project finance). The Bank has also adopted an Environment and Social Policy which serves as a structured approach towards responsible lending. Through this policy, the Bank integrates environmental and social (E&S) risks into its overall credit risk assessment framework, which goes beyond financial risk mitigation. The policy encompasses all the lending transactions of the Bank integrating E&S considerations in its financing activities and establishes a risk-based approach where high value transactions that carry high ESG risks are subject to enhanced evaluation and approval through a specialised team of internal/ external E&S risk assessment experts.

Classification and valuation of the Bank’s investments are carried out in accordance with Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 as updated from time to time.
Level 1: Valuation based on quoted market price: These investments are valued with quoted prices (unadjusted) for identical instruments in active markets that the Bank can access at the measurement date.

The Bank follows settlement date accounting for Investments. In compliance with RBI guidelines, all investments, are categorised as “Fair Value Through Profit & Loss” (‘FVTPL’), “Available for Sale” (‘AFS’) or “Held to Maturity” (‘HTM’) and under sub-category of FVTPL as “Held for Trading” (‘HFT’) at the time of its purchase. All investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures are categorised under a separate category as “Investments in Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures” (‘Subsidiaries and/ or joint ventures’). For the purpose of disclosure in the balance sheet, investments are classified as disclosed in Schedule 8 (‘Investments’) under six groups (a) government securities (b) other approved securities (c) shares (d) debentures and bonds (e) subsidiaries and/or joint ventures and (f) others.
Level 3: Valuation technique with significant unobservable inputs: These investments are valued using valuation techniques where one or more significant inputs are unobservable.

Investments categorised under AFS and FVTPL categories is fair valued on periodical basis as per relevant RBI guidelines. 17.4.3 Advances

17.4.3 Advances
The Bank has in place a Country Risk management policy as part of its Board approved Credit policy, which is based on extant regulatory guidelines and addresses the identification, measurement, monitoring and reporting of country risk. Countries are categorized into seven risk categories, viz. Insignificant, Low Risk, Moderately Low Risk, Moderate Risk, Moderately High Risk, High Risk and Very High Risk. The Bank calculates direct and indirect country risk in line with the Credit policy requirements. Indirect exposure is reckoned at 50% of the exposure in case of countries where the net funded exposure exceeds 1% of the Bank’s total assets. Further, if the net funded exposure of the Bank in respect of each country exceeds 1% of the Bank’s total assets, provisioning is required to be made on exposure to such countries. Depending on the risk category of the country, provisioning is done on a graded scale ranging from 0.25% to 100%.
Accounting and classification
Advances are classified as performing and non-performing based on the relevant RBI guidelines. Advances are stated net of specific provisions, interest in suspense, inter-bank participation certificates issued, direct assignment and bills rediscounted.

Advances are classified as performing and non-performing based on the relevant RBI guidelines. Advances are stated net of specific provisions, interest in suspense, inter-bank participation certificates issued, direct assignment and bills rediscounted.
Assets transferred through direct assignment of cash flows are de-recognised in the Balance Sheet when they are sold (true sale criteria being fully met with) and consideration is received by the Bank. For assets acquired under direct assignment / co-lending arrangements, the appropriation of recoveries and levy of penal interest / charges is in accordance with the contractual terms that have been agreed with the borrower.

The Bank has a Board approved policy for creation, utilization and accounting of contingency provisions. The contingency provision refers to specific provision recognized on the Bank’s standard advances / investments and NFB exposures over and above regulatory provision. The contingency provision will be utilized against creation of specific regulatory provision or provision as per Bank’s Policy. Contingency provisions shall not be reversed by credit to the profit and loss account unless the specific exposures have been fully or partially settled/paid off / written off. Until utilization, the contingency provisions shall not be netted from gross advances but shown separately as ‘Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets’ under ‘Other Liabilities and Provisions Others’ in Schedule 5 of the balance sheet.
Provisioning

Provisioning
Provisions in respect of non-performing advances are made based on management’s assessment of the degree of impairment of the advances, subject to the minimum provisioning level prescribed in relevant RBI guidelines. The specific provision levels for retail non-performing advances are also based on the nature of product and delinquency levels. Specific provisions in respect of non-performing advances are charged to the Profit and Loss account and included under Provisions and Contingencies. In relation to non-performing derivative contracts, as per the extant RBI guidelines, the Bank makes provision for the entire amount of overdue and future receivables relating to positive marked to market value of the said derivative contracts.
The Bank has a Board approved policy for making floating provision, which is in addition to the specific and general provisions made by the Bank. The floating provision is utilised, with the approval of Board and RBI, in case of contingencies which do not arise in the normal course of business and are exceptional and non-recurring in nature and for making specific provision for impaired loans as per the requirement if extant RBI guidelines or any regulatory guidance/instructions. The floating provision created is netted from gross NPAs to arrive at net NPAs.

In respect of loans reported as fraud to RBI the entire amount is provided for over a period not exceeding four quarters starting from the quarter in which fraud has been detected. In respect of loans where there has been delay in reporting the fraud to the RBI, the entire amount is provided immediately.
The Bank considers an account as restructured, where for economic or legal reasons relating to the borrower’s financial difficulty, the Bank grants concessions to the borrower, that the Bank would not otherwise consider. The moratorium granted to the borrowers based on RBI guidelines is not accounted as restructuring of loan. The RBI guidelines on ‘Resolution Framework for COVID-19-related Stress’ provide a prudential framework for resolution plan of certain loans. The borrowers where resolution plan was implemented under these guidelines are classified as standard restructured.

17.4.13 Income taxes
Tax expense comprises of current and deferred tax. Current tax comprises of the amount of tax for the period determined in accordance with the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the rules framed there under. Deferred taxes reflect the impact of timing differences between taxable income and accounting income for the current year and reversal of timing differences of earlier years and carry forward losses. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognised for the future tax consequences of timing differences between the carrying values of assets and liabilities and their respective tax bases, and operating loss carry forwards. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using the enacted or substantively enacted tax rates at the balance sheet date. The impact of changes in deferred tax assets and liabilities is recognised in the profit and loss account.

Deferred tax assets are recognized only to the extent there is reasonable certainty that the assets can be realised in future. Judgment dated September 30, 2020 of the Hon’ble Madras High Court (“MHC”):
The RBI Master Circular on Basel III Capital Regulations, in so far as it relates to issuance and write down of AT-1 Bonds, was challenged before the Division Bench of the Hon’ble MHC in the Writ Petition titled Piyush Bokaria Vs. Reserve Bank of India and Ors., (being W.P. (Civil) 12586 of 2020). The Hon’ble MHC vide its judgment dated September 30, 2020 upheld the validity of the RBI Master Circular in relation to the AT-1 Bonds. Additionally, with respect to the aspect of writing down of AT-1 Bonds, the Hon’ble MHC observed that one of the features of AT-1 Bonds is that they can be written-down before the equity shares bear losses and considering that the Petitioners purchased the AT-1 Bonds in the secondary market, they cannot claim to be ignorant of the terms and conditions thereof. The Hon’ble MHC also noted the loss absorbency feature of the AT-1 Bonds and dismissed the Writ Petition.

The Bank has in place a policy on managing credit risk arising out of unhedged foreign currency exposures of its borrowers. The objective of this policy is to maximize the hedging on foreign currency exposures of borrowers by reviewing their foreign currency product portfolio and encouraging them to hedge the unhedged portion. In line with the policy, assessment of unhedged foreign currency exposure is a part of assessment of borrowers and is undertaken while proposing limits or at the review stage. Additionally, at the time of sanctioning limits for all clients, the Bank stipulates a limit on the unhedged foreign currency exposure of the client (as a % of total foreign currency exposure sanctioned by the Bank) after considering factors such as internal rating of the borrower, size, possibility of natural hedging, sophistication of borrower and maturity of borrower’s financial systems, relative size of unhedged foreign currency exposure with respect to total borrowings of the client, etc. Further, the Bank reviews the unhedged foreign currency exposure across its portfolio on a periodic basis. The Bank also maintains incremental provision and capital towards the unhedged foreign currency exposures of its borrowers in line with the extant RBI guidelines.

The Bank enters into foreign exchange contracts, currency options, forward rate agreements, currency swaps and interest rate swaps with interbank participants and customers. Forward exchange contracts are commitments to buy or sell foreign currency at a future date at the contracted rate. Currency swaps are commitments to exchange cash flows by way of interest/ principal in one currency against another, based on predetermined rates. Interest rate swaps are commitments to exchange fixed and floating interest rate cash flows. The notional amounts of financial instruments of such foreign exchange contracts and derivatives provide a basis for comparison with instruments recognized on the balance sheet but do not necessarily indicate the amounts of future cash flows involved or the current fair value of the instruments and, therefore, do not indicate the Bank’s exposure to credit or price risks. The derivative instruments become favorable (assets) or unfavorable (liabilities) as a result of fluctuations in market rates or prices relative to their terms. Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls with reference to consolidated financial statements, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls with reference to consolidated financial statements to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial control with reference to consolidated financial statement may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.
A Bank’s internal financial controls with reference to consolidated financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of consolidated financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. Accounting and Classification
The Bank determines the fair values of its investments according to the following hierarchy:

The Bank determines the fair values of its investments according to the following hierarchy:
The Bank follows settlement date accounting for Investments. In compliance with RBI guidelines, all investments, are categorised as “Fair Value Through Profit & Loss” (‘FVTPL’), “Available for Sale” (‘AFS’) or “Held to Maturity” (‘HTM’) and under sub-category of FVTPL as “Held for Trading” (‘HFT’) at the time of its purchase. All investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures are categorised under a separate category as “Investments in Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures” (‘Subsidiaries and/ or joint ventures’). For the purpose of disclosure in the balance sheet, investments are classified as disclosed in Schedule 8 (‘Investments’) under six groups (a) government securities (b) other approved securities (c) shares (d) debentures and bonds (e) subsidiaries and/or joint ventures and (f) others.
Level 1: Valuation based on quoted market price: These investments are valued with quoted prices (unadjusted) for identical instruments in active markets that the Bank can access at the measurement date.
Level 2: Valuation based on using observable inputs: These investments are valued with inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1, that are observable, either directly or indirectly.

Level 2: Valuation based on using observable inputs: These investments are valued with inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1, that are observable, either directly or indirectly.
Level 3: Valuation technique with significant unobservable inputs: These investments are valued using valuation techniques where one or more significant inputs are unobservable.
YSIL classifies investments into long term investments and current investments. Investments which are intended to be held for more than one year are classified as long-term investments and investments which are intended to be held for less than one year are classified as current investments. Long-term Investments are stated at cost after deducting provision made, if any, for other than temporary diminution in the value. Current Investments are stated at lower of cost and market/ fair value.
Investments categorised under AFS and FVTPL categories is fair valued on periodical basis as per relevant RBI guidelines. The valuation gains and losses across all performing investments irrespective of classification held under AFS or FVTPL is aggregated. The net appreciation or depreciation is directly credited or debited to AFS reserve or Profit & Loss Account of investments under AFS or FVTPL category respectively.
Purchase and sale transactions in securities are accounted on settlement date.

Purchase and sale transactions in securities are accounted on settlement date.
a) Initial Recognition (Cost of acquisition)
Investments received in lieu of restructured advances scheme are valued in accordance with RBI guidelines. Any diminution in value on these investments is provided for and is not used to set off against appreciation in respect of other performing securities in that category. Depreciation on equity shares acquired and held by the Bank under restructuring scheme is provided as per RBI guidelines.
All investments are measured at fair value on initial recognition, unless facts and circumstances suggest that the fair value is materially different from the acquisition cost, the acquisition cost is the fair value of the assets. In case the fair value of investment is different from cost of acquisition, Day 1 Gain/Loss is recognised in Profit and Loss Account.
Day 1 Loss arising from Level 3 investments is recognised immediately. Any Day 1 gains arising from Level 3 investments is deferred. In case of debt instruments, the Day 1 gain is amortised on a straight-line basis up to the maturity date (or earliest call date for perpetual instruments), while for unquoted equity instruments, the gain is set aside as a liability until the security is listed or derecognised.

Investments classified under the HTM category are carried at cost and any premium or discount over the face value, paid on acquisition, is amortised on a straight -line basis over the remaining period to maturity. Where in the opinion of management, a diminution, other than temporary in the value of investments classified under HTM has taken place, suitable provisions are made. Profit/loss on sale of investments in the ‘Held to Maturity’ category is recognised in the profit and loss account and profit is thereafter appropriated (net of applicable taxes and statutory reserve requirements) to Capital Reserve.
Cost such as brokerage pertaining to investments, paid at the time of acquisition and broken period interest are charged to the profit and loss account as per the RBI guidelines.
Investments in subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures as classified under a separate category “Investments in Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures” is held at acquisition cost. The Bank assesses these investments for impairment on intervals as mentioned in RBI circular. Treasury Bills, Commercial Paper and Certificates of deposit being discounted instruments, are valued at carrying cost.
b) Basis of classification

b) Basis of classification
Investments are classified as per Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 as updated from time to time. Securities that meets SPPI criterion and the Bank intends to hold them till maturity are classified under the HTM category. Securities meets SPPI criterion and the Bank intends to held for sale are classified under AFS category. All other investments excluding investments in subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures, which are not classified in the above categories are classified under the FVTPL (non-HFT) residual category. Held for Trading (HFT) is a separate investment subcategory within FVTPL. Investment in Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures are classified under a separate category as “Investments in Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures”.
PTCs purchased for priority sector lending requirements are valued in accordance with RBI guidelines.
The market/ fair value applied for the purpose of periodical valuation of quoted investments included in the AFS and FVTPL (including HFT) categories is the market price of the scrip as available from the trades/ quotes on the recognised stock exchanges and for Subsidiary General Ledger (‘SGL’) account transactions, the prices as periodically declared by Financial Benchmarks India Pvt. Ltd. (FBIL).

c) Reclassification between categories
The market/ fair value of unquoted government securities included in the AFS and FVTPL (including HFT) category is determined as per the prices published by FBIL. Further, in the case of unquoted bonds, debentures, PTCs (other than priority sector) and preference shares, valuation is carried out by applying an appropriate mark-up (reflecting associated credit risk) over the Yield to Maturity (‘YTM’) rates of government securities. Such mark up and YTM rates applied are as per the relevant rates published by FIMMDA/FBIL.
Reclassification of investments from one category to the other, if done, is in accordance with RBI guidelines. As per RBI guidelines, reclassification between category requires Board of Directors prior approval. Further, reclassification shall also require the prior approval of the Department of Supervision (DoS), RBI.

e) Profit/Loss on sale of Investments
Quoted equity shares are valued at their closing price on a recognised stock exchange. Unquoted equity shares are valued at the break-up value if the latest balance sheet is available, else, at ` 1 per company, as per relevant RBI guidelines.
Cost of investments is computed based on the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) method. Profit/Loss on sale of Investments in the HTM category is recognised in the profit and loss account and profit thereafter is appropriated (net of applicable taxes and statutory reserve requirements) to Capital Reserve. Profit/Loss on sale of investments in FVTPL and non-equity investment under AFS categories is recognised in the Profit and Loss account. For stressed loans transferred to Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC) where the consideration is lower than the net book value (NBV) at the time of transfer, the shortfall is debited to the Profit and Loss Account and spread equally over the financial year. The realised profit, where the cash recovery exceeds the NBV of the stressed loans, the same is credited to Profit and Loss Account. For stressed loans where the consideration received was higher than the NBV at the time of transfer but the cash recovery is lower than the NBV, such excess amount is not reversed in the Profit and Loss Account and the Bank continues to carry forward the same as provision against the Security Receipts (SRs). In effect, the value of SRs is reflected in a manner that the value of SRs is not higher than the NBV of the loans transferred to ARC. The provisioning requirements is as per the extant RBI guidelines applied on each reporting date, taking into account the principle that there should be no provisioning arbitrage between the provisioning on security receipts vis-à-vis the provisioning requirements on the underlying stressed loans, had it stayed in the books. SRs/ PTCs which are not redeemed as at the end of resolution period are fully provided in books of accounts.

f) Accounting for repos / reverse repos/Targeted Long-Term Repo Operations (TLTRO)
Securities sold under agreements to repurchase (Repos) and securities purchased under agreements to resell (Reverse Repos) including liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) with RBI are treated as collateralized borrowing and lending transactions respectively in accordance with RBI (Commercial Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 as updated from time to time. The first leg of the repo transaction is contracted at the prevailing market rates. The difference between consideration amounts of first and second (reversal of first) leg reflects interest and is recognised as interest income/expense over the period of transaction.
Investments in quoted Mutual Fund (MF) Units are valued at the latest repurchase price/NAV declared by the MF. Investments in un-quoted MF Units are valued on the basis of the latest re-purchase price declared by the MF in respect of each particular Scheme.

Transfer to IFR will be lower of the following (i) net profit on sale of investments during the year or (ii) net profit for the year less mandatory appropriations; until the amount of IFR is at least 2 percent of the AFS and FVTPL (including HFT) portfolio, on a continuing basis.
